About: why the classical cavity spectrum diverges and Planck's does not

Source

Concept
Black-body radiation: Planck's law u(f) = (8πf²/c³)·hf/(e^(hf/kT)−1) against the classical Rayleigh–Jeans law u(f) = (8πf²/c³)·kT, where h is Planck's constant and k is Boltzmann's constant.
Serves
Why the classical law is exact at low frequency yet fails at high frequency, and how the peak and the total respond to temperature.
Inquiry
Six committed predictions across the two curves, the peak's position and its height, and the total.
Misconception
"The classical curve is a rough approximation that gets steadily worse."

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealEach of the six gated cards commits an answer before the slider is touched or the answer-bearing readout appears.
Target the misconceptionEach wrong option carries a targeted rebuttal, shown only on selection.
Invariant made visibleThe inset re-plots both laws against the single combination η = hf/kT.
Fixed axesFrequency 0–1.0×10¹⁵ Hz and u 0–2.0×10⁻¹⁵ never rescale, so the peak visibly slides and the dashed curve visibly exits the frame.
Honest limitsThe classical curve is clipped at the frame edge with no cap — it never plateaus — and is given no total, because its integral diverges.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A hole in a hot cavity

Let’s set the scene. A cavity whose walls sit at temperature T glows through a small hole — a black body. On one axis you’ll see two laws for the energy density u(f): the solid Planck curve and the dashed Rayleigh–Jeans curve. Both are plotted on one fixed frame: frequency across, energy density up.

2 · Where do they agree?

Let’s compare the two laws. T is at 6000 K with both curves drawn. Where on the frequency axis do the two curves agree most closely?

3 · The dashed curve rising

Now let’s look at the classical law on its own. Follow the dashed Rayleigh–Jeans curve upward from the origin. What does the curve do at increasing frequencies?

4 · Why the solid curve falls

Why does the Planck curve fall to zero at higher frequencies?

5 · Where the peak moves

Now let’s track the peak. With T at 3000 K, f_max reads about 1.76×10¹⁴ Hz in the Readouts panel. Before you raise T to 6000 K, what do you predict the f_max readout will then show?

6 · How the peak changes

Card 5 pinned down where the peak sits. Now take both of its coordinates together: how does the peak of the Planck curve change with increasing T?

7 · The total under the curve

One more prediction, this time for the whole area under the curve. At 3000 K the total energy density reads about 0.0613 J/m³. Before you double T to 6000 K, what do you predict that readout will become?

8 · The whole difference

So here’s the whole story. The classical law counts the modes correctly and then gives every one the same energy kT; quantising that energy — allowed only in whole units hf — is the entire difference. The line now marked in the inset, η peak = 2.82, is that fixed peak position.

The Physics

Black-body radiation · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A hot cavity glows through a small hole with a spectrum that depends only on its temperature T. This sim plots two laws for that spectrum, the classical Rayleigh–Jeans law and Planck's quantum law, on one fixed frame so you can compare them directly.

What you'll learn

  • How the energy density u(f) is built from two factors: how many standing waves there are, and how much energy each one holds.
  • How the two laws compare as the frequency f and the temperature T change.
  • How the peak frequency and the total energy density depend on T.
  • What the combination η = hf/kT measures.
A cavity with walls at temperature T. The hole is small enough not to disturb the radiation inside.

What's on screen

  • Planck curve (solid cyan): the energy density u(f) from Planck's law.
  • Rayleigh–Jeans curve (dashed amber): the classical law. It is cut off at the top of the frame.
  • f peak (violet marker): where the Planck curve is highest.
  • η inset (top right): both laws against η = hf/kT, with the peak at η = 2.82 marked.
  • Readouts: the peak frequency fmax and the total energy density, both for the Planck curve.
See itShow the whole display at 6000 K. Watch for: a solid cyan and a dashed amber curve on one frame, a violet peak marker, and the η inset at top right.

03

Modes times energy per mode

Both laws build the spectrum the same way: the number of standing-wave modes per unit volume per unit frequency, times the average energy each mode holds.

Count times energy. The two laws differ only in the second factor.

The count, 8πf²/c³ (two polarisations included), grows as f² and is shared by both laws. Classically, equipartition gives every mode the same average energy kT, whatever its frequency:

Rayleigh–Jeans law: the energy density just follows the mode count.

So the dashed curve rises as f² with no turnover. This is the ultraviolet catastrophe. It leaves the top of the frame at 1.61×10¹⁴ Hz for T = 6000 K, and at 2.28×10¹⁴ Hz for 3000 K.

See itLook at the dashed curve at 6000 K. Watch for: the dashed amber curve climbing out of the top of the frame, with no turnover.
04

Quantised energy per mode

In Planck's law a mode of frequency f can hold energy only in whole steps of hf. At temperature T its average energy is then:

Planck's law: the same mode count, a different energy per mode.
  • When hf ≪ kT the steps are tiny next to kT, and the average tends to kT: the classical value.
  • When hf ≫ kT even one step is rarely occupied, and the average falls toward zero.
  • The mode count keeps rising as f², so the product rises and then falls. The peak is at η = hf/kT = 2.82, the root of η = 3(1 − e−η), not at η = 1.
Average energy of one mode in units of kT. At η = 1 it is 58% of kT; at the peak, η = 2.82, it is 18%. The dashed line is the classical value.
See itCompare the two laws at 3000 K. Watch for: the solid curve turning over at the violet peak marker, while the dashed curve keeps rising out of the frame.
05

Agreement and failure are set by η

Divide both laws by 8π(kT)³/h²c³ and f and T appear only through η = hf/kT: Planck's law becomes η³/(eη − 1) and the classical law becomes η². The two limits of the bracket in Planck's law:

Planck's law tends to the classical law as η → 0.
  • The ratio (classical)/(Planck) is (eη − 1)/η: 1.05 at η = 0.1, 1.72 at η = 1, 5.6 at the peak.
  • At the right edge of the frame η = 8.0 at 6000 K, where the classical value is about 370 times too high, and η = 16.0 at 3000 K, where it is about 5.5×10⁵ times too high.
  • Raising T lowers η at any given f, so the laws agree over a wider range of f. At η = 0.1 that range ends at f = 1.25×10¹³ Hz for 6000 K.

Because the η inset has no T in it, it does not move when T changes.

See itSweep T from 3000 K to 6000 K and back. Watch for: the main plot changing while the η inset (top right) stays still.
06

Where the peak sits

The peak of the Planck curve is at ηp = 2.8214. Because ηp is a pure number, the peak frequency is proportional to T:

The peak of u per unit frequency, the curve the sim plots.
  • Doubling T doubles fmax.
  • The height at the peak goes as T³, so doubling T raises it eightfold.
T

This slider moves the sim's temperature too.

See itSweep T from 3000 K to 6000 K. Watch for: the violet peak marker moving right and up, and the peak frequency doubling from 1.76×10¹⁴ to 3.53×10¹⁴ Hz.
07

How the total scales

The total energy density is the area under the Planck curve. Substituting η = hf/kT pulls (kT)⁴ out of the integral, so the total is proportional to T⁴:

The Planck integral, with a = 7.566×10⁻¹⁶ J m⁻³ K⁻⁴.
  • Doubling T multiplies the total by 2⁴ = 16: from 0.0613 J/m³ at 3000 K to 0.9805 J/m³ at 6000 K.
  • The classical curve has no total. Its integral grows without limit as the upper frequency is raised, so the readout shows Planck's value only.

This is energy per unit volume inside the cavity. The power per unit area leaving the hole is (c/4)aT⁴ = σT⁴, with σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

See itSweep T from 3000 K to 6000 K. Watch for: the Total energy density readout rising from 0.0613 to 0.9805 J/m³.
08

Where it matters

fmax = 5.879×10¹⁰ Hz K⁻¹ × T. The sim's slider covers only the shaded strip; the other bodies lie outside it but follow the same law.
  • The Sun has an effective temperature of 5772 K. Its per-frequency peak is at 3.39×10¹⁴ Hz, in the near infrared.
  • An incandescent filament at about 2800 K, treated as an ideal black body, puts only about 8% of its power into visible light. Most is infrared.
  • The cosmic microwave background at 2.725 K peaks at 1.6×10¹¹ Hz, in the microwave band. The COBE satellite found its spectrum matches a black body to better than 1 part in 10⁴ of the peak.
Go deeper: the peak in frequency and in wavelength
  • The curve per unit wavelength is a different function, so its maximum falls elsewhere: λmaxT = 2.898×10⁻³ m K, while c/fmax = 5.10×10⁻³ m K / T.
  • For the Sun that is 502 nm for the per-wavelength peak and 883 nm for the per-frequency peak the sim plots.
09

Summary

In one line. Both laws use the same mode count, 8πf²/c³, and differ only in the energy per mode: kT classically, hf/(eη − 1) in Planck's law, with η = hf/kT.

Key points

  • The classical law rises as f² without limit and has no total.
  • Planck's law turns over at η = 2.82, so fmax = 5.879×10¹⁰ Hz K⁻¹ × T.
  • The total energy density is aT⁴.
  • The classical law is the η → 0 limit of Planck's law.

Common mix-ups

  • "There are fewer high-frequency modes, so the curve falls." The count keeps growing as f². The fall comes from the average energy per mode.
  • "The peak is at hf = kT." The peak is at η = 2.82, where the rising count and the falling energy per mode balance.
  • "A hotter cavity only makes the curve taller." The peak also moves to higher frequency, in proportion to T.

Things to try on your own

  • Read fmax at 3000 K and at 6000 K, and check that the ratio is 2.
  • Read the total at 3000 K and at 6000 K, and check that the ratio is 16.
  • Move T slowly and watch where the dashed curve leaves the top of the frame. Compare 3000 K with 6000 K.
